processes:
WHAT IT IS
Processes are running instances of programs. Windows has a small set of expected 'core' processes (System, smss.exe, csrss.exe, wininit.exe, services.exe, svchost.exe, lsass.exe, winlogon.exe, explorer.exe) with a known parent-child tree.

WHY IT MATTERS
Malware often disguises itself using legitimate-sounding process names, or spawns from an unusual parent (e.g. svchost.exe not under services.exe, or Word spawning powershell.exe).

IOCs TO LOOK FOR
- A core process name running from the wrong path (e.g. C:\Users\...\svchost.exe)
- Unexpected parent-child relationships (winword.exe -> cmd.exe -> powershell.exe)
- Processes with no icon/description or unsigned binaries
- Unusually high number of svchost.exe instances or odd command-line arguments
autoruns:
WHAT IT IS
Autoruns are anything configured to start automatically: Registry Run/RunOnce keys, Startup folder items, services, scheduled tasks, and more. Sysinternals Autoruns aggregates all of these in one place.

WHY IT MATTERS
Persistence is a core attacker goal - if their code doesn't survive reboot, they lose access. Run keys are one of the simplest and most common persistence techniques.

IOCs TO LOOK FOR
- Entries pointing to binaries in Temp, AppData, or Downloads
- Unsigned or 'Not verified' publishers
- Recently added entries not present in your baseline
- Obscure or misspelled names mimicking legitimate software
services:
WHAT IT IS
Windows Services run in the background, often as LocalSystem, and can be configured to auto-start on boot via the Service Control Manager (SCM).

WHY IT MATTERS
Services are attractive to attackers for both persistence (auto-start on reboot) and privilege escalation (running as LocalSystem). 'sc qc <name>' or the WMI/CIM Win32_Service class are the key ways to see the actual binary path - Get-Service alone does not show it.

IOCs TO LOOK FOR
- Service binary path pointing outside C:\Windows\System32\ (e.g. Temp, AppData, Users)
- Newly created services not in your baseline (Sysmon/Security Event ID 7045)
- Services with no description or an unfamiliar display name
- 'Not verified' publisher when checked in Autoruns
tasks_cron:
WHAT IT IS
Scheduled Tasks (Windows) and Cron jobs (Linux) run commands on a defined schedule or trigger, without requiring a running process the whole time.

WHY IT MATTERS
An attacker can create a task/cron entry that periodically re-establishes a foothold, making it a common persistence mechanism that's easy to overlook compared to services.

IOCs TO LOOK FOR
- Tasks/cron jobs referencing scripts in Temp/AppData/tmp
- Tasks that run at logon or at short, unusual intervals
- Task names mimicking system tasks
- Recently modified crontab entries or task XML files
eventlogs:
WHAT IT IS
Windows Event Logs record system, security, and application events. Key logs: Security (logons: 4624, 4625), System (service installs: 7045), Application.

WHY IT MATTERS
Event Logs are often the only record of what happened on a system, especially after an attacker cleans up files. Correlating Event IDs over time reconstructs the attack timeline.

IOCs TO LOOK FOR
- Repeated 4625 (failed logon) followed by a 4624 (success) - possible brute force
- 4720 (user account created) outside change windows
- 7045 (service installed) shortly before/after suspicious network activity
- Logs that were cleared (Event ID 1102)
sysmon:
WHAT IT IS
Sysmon (Sysinternals) is a Windows system service and driver that logs detailed process creation, network connection, and file change events - far more detail than default Windows logging.

WHY IT MATTERS
Sysmon's 'superpower' is correlation: every event includes a ProcessGuid/ProcessId you can pivot on to build the full picture of what a process did (network connections, files touched, child processes).

IOCs TO LOOK FOR
- Event ID 1 (process creation) with unusual command-line arguments
- Event ID 3 (network connection) from an unexpected process
- Event ID 7045 correlated with a new Sysmon Event ID 1 for the same binary
- LSASS access attempts (credential dumping)
registry:
WHAT IT IS
The Registry is a hierarchical database of Windows configuration, organized into Hives (HKLM, HKCU, etc.), Keys, and Values. Services, Run keys, and Winlogon settings all live here.

WHY IT MATTERS
Many persistence mechanisms ultimately write to the Registry. HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\<name> holds each service's ImagePath, Start type, and account - the same data 'sc qc' shows you.

IOCs TO LOOK FOR
- ImagePath values pointing to Temp/AppData/Users
- Start value of 2 (Auto) on an unfamiliar service
- Modified Winlogon Shell/Userinit values (should be explorer.exe / userinit.exe only)
- Unexpected Run/RunOnce entries
network:
WHAT IT IS
Active network connections show what's currently talking to what, including local/remote IP:port and the owning process ID.

WHY IT MATTERS
Command-and-control (C2) beacons and reverse shells show up here as outbound connections from unexpected processes to unfamiliar remote hosts.

IOCs TO LOOK FOR
- Outbound connections from processes that shouldn't need network access (e.g. notepad.exe)
- Connections to unusual high ports or to raw IPs with no reverse DNS
- Repeated beaconing to the same remote host at regular intervals
- ESTABLISHED connections tied to a PID with no matching legitimate process name
